title: Learn to make your characters say what they don’t mean, and watch your story catch fire.
use_cases: Use when dialogue feels flat or lacks emotional depth
Implement when characters are being too direct or honest in their communication
Configure when trying to reveal internal character conflict without explicit exposition
Use when drafting scenes to create tension through silences and subtext
content:
That blank page stares back, doesn’t it? You’ve written a conversation, the words are all there, but it feels… flat. Like two mannequins trading information, every line a direct answer to the last. There’s a hollowness to it, a feeling that you’re just moving the plot along instead of revealing the messy, beating hearts of your characters. The truth is, the most powerful dialogue whispers between the lines, in the silences and the deflections. I’m going to walk you through seven concrete methods to weave that magic into your own work, turning hollow exchanges into scenes that pulse with unspoken tension.

I feel this in my bones. For fifteen years, I swam in the ink of student manuscripts at a university here in New York. I saw the same struggle again and again: brilliant ideas hobbled by dialogue that was too honest, too direct. Now, as an editor, I see it in manuscripts from writers of all levels. We are taught to communicate clearly in life, but in fiction, clarity is often the enemy of truth. The real human stuff—the fear, the longing, the resentment—hides beneath the surface. Our job is to give it a voice without letting it speak its name.

This isn’t about learning a trick. It’s about learning to listen—to your characters, and to the rhythm of real human interaction. We are going to treat this like a craft, a skill you can develop with intention and practice. Let’s get our hands dirty.
